clue.text: Refusal, say, to be put in home

indicators.note: the word for 'say' is placed inside the word for 'home', which opens up to take it

parts.note: native means belonging to one's home, as in one's native land
EG (exempli gratia) is the abbreviation meaning 'for example', i.e. 'say'

explanation.surface: A refusal, for instance, being taken into a care home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refusal, say' looks like one unit, but 'say' belongs to the wordplay as EG.
explanation.definitionFit: A negative is a no, a denial given in reply to a request.

clue.text: First of parr following river leading to ocean

indicators.note: the piece from 'First of parr' comes after the river in the answer

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland, and another on the England–Wales border

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word parr is wanted

explanation.surface: A young salmon (a parr) heads down a river to the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The deep' is a poetic name for the sea, so deep stands for ocean.

clue.text: Gift's frilly, capturing bridegroom's heart

indicators.note: the word for frilly closes around and holds the other piece

parts.note: lacy means trimmed with lace, frilly

indicators.note: the central two letters of the ten-letter word bridegroom are taken

explanation.surface: A wedding present is fussy and lacy, and wins the groom's affection.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridegroom has ten letters, so its heart is the middle pair, E and G.
explanation.definitionFit: A legacy is something bequeathed in a will, a gift left to an heir.

clue.text: Panic with tee shot in game

indicators.note: shot in the sense of ruined or wrecked tells us these letters are shattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: A golfer panics over a tee shot during a round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' looks like the golf stroke from the tee, but it is the anagram signal on PANIC and TEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Patience is a card game for one player, called solitaire in America.

clue.text: Stay quiet, taking in speaker and this writer

indicators.note: the word for quiet swallows the other pieces inside it

parts.note: mum means silent, as in 'keep mum'
an orator is a public speaker
the writer of the clue refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: An order to stay silent, letting a speaker and the author in.
explanation.definitionFit: A moratorium is a stay, a temporary suspension of an activity or legal obligation.

clue.text: Surreptitiously taken or lifted, even nicked initially

definitions.text: Surreptitiously taken or lifted, even nicked initially

indicators.note: the first letter of each of the six preceding words is taken in turn

explanation.surface: Something has been taken on the sly, lifted or even pinched.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and, by its initials, the wordplay. 'Lifted' and 'nicked' are British slang for stolen.
explanation.definitionFit: Stolen goods are those taken surreptitiously, lifted or nicked by a thief.

clue.text: Religion's leader always facing extreme cleric

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter, here of religion

parts.note: ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'
an end is an extremity, the extreme point

explanation.surface: A church head is constantly up against a fanatical priest.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverend is a member of the clergy, a title for a priest or minister.

clue.text: Show of French dive around beginning of cabaret

parts.note: de is French for 'of'

indicators.note: the word for dive goes round the letter taken from cabaret

parts.note: a dive is a sleazy place, a pit

indicators.note: only the first letter of the word cabaret is wanted

explanation.surface: A French show staged in a seedy club, built round a cabaret.
explanation.definitionFit: To depict is to show or portray something in a picture or words.

clue.text: Assumes trouble approaching uneven bits of paths

parts.note: ado is fuss or trouble, as in 'without further ado'

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters (first, third, fifth) of the word paths

explanation.surface: Someone assumes trouble is coming along the bumpy patches of a path.
explanation.definitionFit: To adopt a manner or position is to assume it or take it on.

clue.text: Breathe in and talk softly

parts.note: gas is idle chatter, so to gas is to talk
p (piano) is the musical marking for softly

explanation.surface: Inhaling, then speaking in a whisper.
explanation.definitionFit: To gasp is to draw in breath sharply, as in shock.

clue.text: Fit old man's back caught in elastic

indicators.note: back means the word for old man is read in reverse

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father, one's old man

indicators.note: the letter for caught goes inside the word for elastic

parts.note: pliable means flexible, elastic
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A fit old man hurts his back, snagged in a stretchy cord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' looks like an adjective about the old man, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Applicable means suitable or relevant, fitting the case.

clue.text: Loosely could give large hint

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels
to imply is to hint or suggest

explanation.surface: A loose suggestion that a big hint might be dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Limply means slackly, without firmness, so loosely.

clue.text: In the flesh, 'tight' describes Queen's playing

indicators.note: describes in its old sense of drawing round, so the word for tight encircles the other pieces

parts.note: tight friends are close, pally
ER (Elizabeth Regina) is the Queen, and the 's adds an S
on means playing or performing, as an actor is on

explanation.surface: A tipsy commentator describes the Queen's performance in person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tight' suggests drunk, but here it means close friends. 'describes' means 'goes round', as a compass describes a circle.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something personally means doing it oneself, in person rather than by proxy.

clue.text: Puzzle of fleece uncovered

parts.note: to fleece someone is to swindle or con them
found means discovered or uncovered

explanation.surface: The mystery of a sheep's coat brought to light.
explanation.definitionFit: To confound is to bewilder or perplex, to puzzle someone.

clue.text: Vinegar needed to trap flipping bug

indicators.note: flipping means turning over, so the caught letters are read backwards
the clue words vinegar needed hold the letters within them, caught across the word gap

explanation.surface: Vinegar is used to catch an annoying insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bug' looks like the insect being trapped, but it is the verb meaning annoy.
explanation.definitionFit: To bug someone is to irritate them; to enrage is to make them furious.

clue.text: Fine work about block being turned

parts.note: go means work, as a machine goes

indicators.note: turned around, so the words for about and block are read backwards

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a mass is a solid lump or block

explanation.surface: Delicate craftsmanship involving a block being shaped on a lathe.
explanation.definitionFit: Gossamer means extremely light and delicate, like a spider's thread, hence fine.

clue.text: Dashes, holding iron over suits

indicators.note: the word for dashes holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: a dash is a small amount, a bit

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the symbol for iron is read backwards

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: Someone hurries off with an iron to press their suits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dashes' suggests rushing, and 'suits' clothes, but they are bits and the verb 'is right for'.
explanation.definitionFit: If something befits you it is proper or appropriate for you, it suits you.

clue.text: Small smalls protecting right stuff?

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing sizes

indicators.note: the word for smalls wraps round the letter for right

parts.note: smalls is British slang for underwear, undies

explanation.surface: Tiny underwear guarding something essential.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smalls' is British slang for underclothes. The question mark admits that 'stuff' is a loose, playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sundries are miscellaneous odds and ends, assorted bits of stuff.

clue.text: Turn red accepting one's a bit obscene

indicators.note: the word for turning red takes the other piece into itself

parts.note: to blush is to go red in the face
one is the Roman numeral I; the 's is 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition

explanation.surface: Someone goes red on admitting they're slightly smutty.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue means risqué or smutty, so a tinge of blue means mildly indecent.

clue.text: Fall backwards clutching old useless support

indicators.note: the reversed word for fall grips the other pieces inside it
the word for fall is written in reverse

parts.note: a lapse is a fall or decline, as in a lapse in standards
U/S (unserviceable) is a British abbreviation for useless

explanation.surface: Someone tumbles backwards gripping an old, broken crutch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backwards' gives ESPAL. U/S, short for unserviceable, is British shorthand for broken or useless; 'support' is the noun, backing for a cause.
explanation.definitionFit: Espousal of a cause is its adoption and backing, i.e. support for it.

clue.text: Shut up keeping warmth in cover

indicators.note: the word for shut up holds the word for warmth within it

parts.note: sh is the call for silence
heat is warmth

explanation.surface: Be quiet, and keep the warmth in under a blanket.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath is a close-fitting case or covering, as for a sword blade.

clue.text: Pong, a not quite fresh kind

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell, a pong

indicators.note: the final letter of the word for fresh is lopped off, leaving it incomplete

parts.note: new means fresh

explanation.surface: A smell that's a bit stale, of some kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pong' is British slang for a stink, as is 'hum'. 'kind' looks like a noun, sort, but it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Humane means compassionate and considerate, i.e. kind.

clue.text: Sharpens head of tool getting blunt

parts.note: to hone a blade is to sharpen it

indicators.note: only the first letter of the word tool is taken

explanation.surface: Someone puts an edge on a tool whose tip has grown dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blunt' looks like dull, the opposite of sharpened, but it means frank.
explanation.definitionFit: A blunt person is frank and plain-spoken, telling the truth openly.

clue.text: On a sea trip waving farewell

indicators.note: waving suggests movement back and forth, so the letters of the four words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone on a cruise waves goodbye from the deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'waving farewell' reads as one phrase, but 'waving' is the anagram signal and 'farewell' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A farewell is a parting, the act of going separate ways.

clue.text: Sailor heading north for mountain lake

indicators.note: heading means going in front, so the word for sailor leads the letter for north

parts.note: a tar (Jack Tar) is an old word for a sailor
N is the compass abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A sailor travels north to a lake in the hills.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarn is a small lake in a mountain hollow, especially in northern England.

clue.text: Precious time with two sweethearts?

parts.note: the heart of the word sweet is its middle letter, E, so two of them give a pair of Es

explanation.surface: A treasured moment shared with a pair of lovers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweethearts' is read as 'sweet hearts': the centre of 'sweet' is E, and two of them give EE.
explanation.definitionFit: Precious can mean affectedly refined, which is what twee means: overly cute or quaint.

clue.text: Prattle endlessly, detaining former PM

indicators.note: detaining means holding, so the words prattle endlessly keep the letters inside them

explanation.surface: Chattering on and on while holding up an ex-premier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' tempts one to trim a word, but it is part of the text in which the answer sits.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement Attlee was the British Labour Prime Minister from 1945 to 1951.

clue.text: Ran humiliated being a non-starter

indicators.note: a non-starter here is a word missing its first letter, so the word for humiliated loses its opening letter

parts.note: chastened means humbled or subdued, made to feel humiliated

explanation.surface: A runner, shamed, turned out not to start the race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran' looks like a racing word alongside 'non-starter', but it is the definition, meaning hurried.
explanation.definitionFit: Hastened means hurried or moved quickly, so it can stand for ran.
